statement.text:
Particles from the Sun
Treat the Sun as a blackbody with mass \(M=2.00\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}\), radius \(R=7.00\times10^8\,\mathrm m\), luminosity \(L=3.85\times10^{26}\,\mathrm W\), and Earth distance \(d=1.50\times10^{11}\,\mathrm m\). Use \(c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}\), \(h=6.63\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}\), \(k_B=1.38\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J/K}\), \(\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{W/(m^2K^4)}\), \(G=6.67\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{SI}\), and \(m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}\). A cell of area \(A\) is normal to sunlight. In the Wien approximation its received power per frequency interval is \(u(\nu)=AR^2d^{-2}(2\pi h/c^2)\nu^3e^{-h\nu/(k_BT_s)}\). Integrals of polynomial times exponential may be evaluated by integration by parts.
A1. Solar surface temperature
Find the blackbody surface temperature.
A2. Incident cell power
Integrate the Wien spectrum to find total incident power.
A3. Photon spectrum
Find the photon number per unit time per unit frequency.
A4. Useful cell power
A photon with energy at least band gap \(E_g=h\nu_g\) supplies useful energy \(E_g\). Other photons supply none. Put \(x_g=E_g/(k_BT_s)\). Find output power.
A5. Efficiency function
Find the efficiency as a function of dimensionless gap.
A6. Efficiency graph
Sketch efficiency, marking the values and slopes at zero gap and at infinite gap.
A7. Best gap and efficiency
Find the cubic for the optimum gap, estimate its root to within \(\pm0.25\), and calculate maximum efficiency.
A8. Silicon efficiency
For silicon use \(E_g=1.11\,\mathrm{eV}\). Calculate efficiency.
A9. Gravitational solar energy
For uniform solar density, find total gravitational potential energy.
A10. Kelvin-Helmholtz lifetime
Assuming constant luminosity and contraction from negligible initial density, estimate the longest shining time supported by gravitational energy.
B1. Solar neutrino flux
The net reaction \(4\,{}^1\mathrm H\to{}^4\mathrm{He}+2e^++2\nu_e\) releases \(\Delta E=4.0\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm J\). Ignore energy carried away by neutrinos. Find neutrino flux at Earth.
B2. Converted neutrino fraction
Detector efficiency for converted \(\nu_x\) is one sixth of that for \(\nu_e\). Without conversion it would count \(N_1\) per year, but observes \(N_2\). Find the converted fraction.
B3. Energy transferred to an electron
An initially resting electron receives energy from a neutrino, then loses energy at constant rate \(\alpha\) in water of refractive index \(n>1\). It emits Cherenkov radiation for \(\Delta t\). Find the transferred energy.
B4. Core temperature from line broadening
Electron capture \({}^7\mathrm{Be}+e^-\to{}^7\mathrm{Li}+\nu_e\) gives rest-source neutrino energy \(E_\nu=1.44\times10^{-13}\,\mathrm J\). Thermal Be nuclei of mass \(11.65\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}\) give rms energy width \(5.54\times10^{-17}\,\mathrm J\). Find their rms speed and core temperature.

children.text: Integrate photon rate above the threshold and multiply by \(E_g\): \[P_{out}=\frac{2\pi AR^2(k_BT_s)^4}{d^2c^2h^3}x_g(x_g^2+2x_g+2)e^{-x_g}.\]
The curve starts at \(\eta(0)=0\) with slope \(1/3\), rises to one maximum, then tends to zero with slope tending to zero from below. Both endpoints have zero efficiency.
Differentiation gives \(x_0^3-x_0^2-2x_0-2=0\). Its positive root is \(x_0\simeq2.27\), with \(\eta_{max}\simeq0.457\).
Build the sphere shell by shell, integrating \(-GM(r)\,dM/r\). The result is \(\Omega=-3GM^2/(5R)\).
\(\tau_{KH}=|\Omega|/L=3GM^2/(5RL)\simeq1.88\times10^7\) years, far below the solar-system age.
There are two neutrinos per reaction, giving \(\Phi_\nu=2L/(4\pi d^2\Delta E)=6.8\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{m^{-2}s^{-1}}\).
B3. Energy transferred to an electron

Emission stops when \(v=c/n\), leaving total energy \(m_ec^2n/\sqrt{n^2-1}\). Add \(\alpha\Delta t\), then subtract the initial rest energy: \[E_{imp}=\alpha\Delta t+m_ec^2\left(\frac n{\sqrt{n^2-1}}-1\right).\]
B4. Core temperature from line broadening

The line-of-sight Doppler width obeys \(\Delta E_{rms}/E_\nu=v_{z,rms}/c\). Isotropy gives \(V_{rms}=\sqrt3v_{z,rms}=2.01\times10^5\,\mathrm{m/s}\). From \(mV_{rms}^2/2=3k_BT_c/2\), \(T_c=1.13\times10^7\,\mathrm K\).

solution.text:
Particles from the Sun
A1. Solar surface temperature
\(L=4\pi R^2\sigma T_s^4\), so \(T_s=(L/(4\pi R^2\sigma))^{1/4}\simeq5760\,\mathrm K\).
A2. Incident cell power
With \(x=h\nu/(k_BT_s)\), \(\int_0^\infty x^3e^{-x}dx=6\). Hence \[P_{in}=\frac{12\pi AR^2(k_BT_s)^4}{d^2c^2h^3}.\]
A3. Photon spectrum
Divide spectral power by \(h\nu\): \[n_\gamma(\nu)=\frac{2\pi AR^2}{d^2c^2}\nu^2e^{-h\nu/(k_BT_s)}.\]
A4. Useful cell power
Integrate photon rate above the threshold and multiply by \(E_g\): \[P_{out}=\frac{2\pi AR^2(k_BT_s)^4}{d^2c^2h^3}x_g(x_g^2+2x_g+2)e^{-x_g}.\]
A5. Efficiency function
\[\eta(x_g)=\frac{x_g(x_g^2+2x_g+2)e^{-x_g}}6.\]
A6. Efficiency graph
The curve starts at \(\eta(0)=0\) with slope \(1/3\), rises to one maximum, then tends to zero with slope tending to zero from below. Both endpoints have zero efficiency.
A7. Best gap and efficiency
Differentiation gives \(x_0^3-x_0^2-2x_0-2=0\). Its positive root is \(x_0\simeq2.27\), with \(\eta_{max}\simeq0.457\).
A8. Silicon efficiency
\(k_BT_s\simeq0.496\,\mathrm{eV}\), so \(x_g\simeq2.24\) and \(\eta_{Si}\simeq0.457\).
A9. Gravitational solar energy
Build the sphere shell by shell, integrating \(-GM(r)\,dM/r\). The result is \(\Omega=-3GM^2/(5R)\).
A10. Kelvin-Helmholtz lifetime
\(\tau_{KH}=|\Omega|/L=3GM^2/(5RL)\simeq1.88\times10^7\) years, far below the solar-system age.
B1. Solar neutrino flux
There are two neutrinos per reaction, giving \(\Phi_\nu=2L/(4\pi d^2\Delta E)=6.8\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{m^{-2}s^{-1}}\).
B2. Converted neutrino fraction
\(N_2=N_1(1-f)+N_1f/6\), so \(f=(6/5)(1-N_2/N_1)\).
B3. Energy transferred to an electron
Emission stops when \(v=c/n\), leaving total energy \(m_ec^2n/\sqrt{n^2-1}\). Add \(\alpha\Delta t\), then subtract the initial rest energy: \[E_{imp}=\alpha\Delta t+m_ec^2\left(\frac n{\sqrt{n^2-1}}-1\right).\]
B4. Core temperature from line broadening
The line-of-sight Doppler width obeys \(\Delta E_{rms}/E_\nu=v_{z,rms}/c\). Isotropy gives \(V_{rms}=\sqrt3v_{z,rms}=2.01\times10^5\,\mathrm{m/s}\). From \(mV_{rms}^2/2=3k_BT_c/2\), \(T_c=1.13\times10^7\,\mathrm K\).
